purpose: Answers the question a client actually asks when they see a gap: 'if we turn this on, what breaks?' controls.json already says what a control is, why it matters and how to remediate it. Nothing in this repo said what enabling it will DO to the people who use the tenant, and that is the question that decides whether a remediation gets scheduled or quietly dropped.
note: Impact clusters. Fourteen separate 'enable auditing' controls have the same operational impact — none — and writing fourteen paragraphs saying so would be noise pretending to be diligence. So the content lives in archetypes and every control names one. Where a control's impact genuinely differs from its archetype it carries an Override, merged over the archetype field by field. A control with no entry renders 'Operational impact not documented' rather than inheriting a default: an unwritten impact statement must never masquerade as 'no impact', because 'no impact' is the answer that gets a change approved.
fields: Effort describes the SHAPE of the work — Single setting / Policy change / Staged rollout / Discovery first / Project / License purchase / Review only — and deliberately never an hour figure. An invented hour count is a promise the tool cannot keep and the first thing a client holds you to; the shape of the work is something the archetype genuinely determines, and it is what decides whether a change goes in tonight or needs a change window. Summary is the one-line answer. Users is what the people using the tenant notice. Admins is the work the change creates or removes. Watchouts is what actually goes wrong, drawn from the failure that happens in practice rather than the theoretical one. Reversible says whether backing the change out restores the previous state.

none-visible.Summary: No user-visible change. Turns on recording or detection that runs behind the tenant.
none-visible.Users: Nothing. No prompts, no blocked actions, no changed behavior.
none-visible.Admins: One configuration change. Data begins accumulating from the moment it is enabled and not before — it is not retroactive, so enabling it during an incident does not recover the history you wanted.
none-visible.Watchouts: The common failure is assuming it was already on and only discovering otherwise when the logs are needed. Verify after enabling rather than trusting the setting page.
none-visible.Reversible: Yes — disabling restores the prior state, though the data collected in between remains.

admin-review-workload.Summary: No user-visible change, but it creates recurring work for whoever owns the tenant.
admin-review-workload.Admins: Generates alerts, reviews or a queue that someone has to actually work. The control is only worth its cost if that ownership is assigned; an unread alert queue scores the same as the gap it replaced but costs more.
admin-review-workload.Watchouts: Alert fatigue. Tune thresholds before enabling broadly, or the first noisy week trains everyone to ignore it.

auth-prompt.Summary: Users get an extra step at sign-in, and a one-time registration before that.
auth-prompt.Users: A registration prompt on next sign-in, then an approval step on subsequent sign-ins that are not covered by an existing session.
auth-prompt.Admins: Registration campaign to run, and a help-desk spike for the first week — lost phones, users who registered on a device they no longer have, shared-account holders who never registered at all.
auth-prompt.Watchouts: Service accounts and shared mailboxes signed in interactively will break at cutover. Inventory them first and exclude deliberately, with the exclusions documented — an undocumented exclusion is indistinguishable from a gap at audit.
auth-prompt.Reversible: Yes, but registrations already collected stay, which is the point.

auth-hardware.Summary: Affected users need a specific credential — a security key, a platform authenticator or a certificate — and cannot sign in without it.
auth-hardware.Users: Cannot sign in from anywhere the required credential is not present. That is the security value and also the entire risk.
auth-hardware.Admins: Procurement and enrollment before enforcement, not after. Enroll every affected account, verify each one has signed in with the new method, then enforce.
auth-hardware.Watchouts: Locking out every administrator simultaneously is a real and recoverable-only-by-Microsoft outcome. Configure and verify break-glass accounts excluded from the policy before enforcing, and test the exclusion works.
auth-hardware.Reversible: Yes, provided you retain a path into the tenant to reverse it.

legacy-client-break.Summary: Old clients, devices and scripts stop connecting. This is the highest-breakage change in the tenant and the one most worth making.
legacy-client-break.Users: Anyone on an outdated client, an old phone mail app or a device that has not been updated in years loses access until they move to a modern client.
legacy-client-break.Admins: Run the sign-in logs filtered to the legacy protocol for at least 30 days first — that report is the change plan. Multifunction printers, scan-to-email, line-of-business applications and monitoring scripts are the usual occupants, and they rarely appear in any inventory.
legacy-client-break.Watchouts: The device nobody remembers is the one that breaks. Scan-to-email on the copier and the backup system's alert mailer are the two that get discovered by their absence.
legacy-client-break.Reversible: Yes, but every affected client stays broken until it is individually reconfigured, so a rollback does not restore service on its own.

mail-flow-latency.Summary: Mail is inspected before delivery, so some messages arrive minutes later than they used to.
mail-flow-latency.Users: Attachment-heavy mail can be delayed while it is analyzed. Users who expect a document to arrive as they are on the phone about it will notice.
mail-flow-latency.Admins: Set expectations before enabling — the support ticket is 'email is slow', not 'security is working'. Dynamic delivery, where the license allows it, removes most of the perceived delay.
mail-flow-latency.Watchouts: Time-critical automated mail — one-time passcodes, dispatch notifications, alerting — is where delay becomes a business problem rather than an annoyance. Identify those senders and route them deliberately.

mail-flow-quarantine.Summary: More mail is held rather than delivered, so somebody has to release the mail that should not have been.
mail-flow-quarantine.Users: Legitimate mail lands in quarantine instead of the inbox. Without end-user release enabled, they cannot get it themselves.
mail-flow-quarantine.Admins: A quarantine to work daily for the first few weeks, and a stated process for release requests. Enable end-user quarantine notifications so the volume does not land entirely on the help desk.
mail-flow-quarantine.Watchouts: Newsletters, invoicing systems and recruiters generate most false positives. Tune with a real sample rather than pre-emptively allow-listing domains, which is how a bypass gets created and then forgotten.

mail-delivery-risk.Summary: Changes how other mail systems treat mail claiming to be from your domain. Configured wrongly, legitimate mail from the organization stops being delivered anywhere.
mail-delivery-risk.Users: Nothing, when it is right. When it is wrong, recipients stop receiving mail from the organization and the organization is usually the last to know.
mail-delivery-risk.Admins: Stage it. Publish in monitoring mode, read the aggregate reports for several weeks until every legitimate sender is identified and authenticated, then tighten. Every third-party service that sends on the organization's behalf — marketing platform, ticketing system, accounting package, e-signature — must be authenticated first.
mail-delivery-risk.Watchouts: Moving straight to an enforcing policy without a monitoring period is the single most common way to break a client's outbound mail. The damage is invisible from inside the tenant: sent items look normal.
mail-delivery-risk.Reversible: Yes, and it takes effect as fast as DNS propagates — but mail rejected in the meantime is gone, not queued.

forwarding-break.Summary: Automatic forwarding out of the tenant stops working, including the forwarding people set up for legitimate reasons.
forwarding-break.Users: Anyone forwarding work mail to a personal account, a colleague at a partner firm or an external ticketing system loses that flow with no notification.
forwarding-break.Admins: Enumerate existing forwarding first — the assessment's named-findings list does this — and contact each owner before enforcing. Most legitimate cases have a supported alternative: a mail-enabled contact, a shared mailbox with delegated access, or a connector.
forwarding-break.Watchouts: Practices that route mail to an answering service or an external bookkeeper break silently. Nobody reports missing mail they never saw; it surfaces weeks later as a missed invoice.
forwarding-break.Reversible: Yes, but each individual forwarding rule has to be recreated.

external-collab-friction.Summary: Guests and external organizations lose access or gain extra steps.
external-collab-friction.Users: Internal users may no longer be able to invite external collaborators themselves. External participants may be prompted to authenticate where they were not before, or lose access entirely.
external-collab-friction.Admins: An invitation request process, and an allow-list to maintain if the restriction is domain-based.
external-collab-friction.Watchouts: Active client and vendor projects break at cutover. Enumerate existing guests and the sites they use before restricting, and stage by domain rather than tenant-wide where the setting allows.
external-collab-friction.Reversible: Yes, though guest objects removed as part of the cleanup have to be re-invited and re-granted.

sharing-restriction.Summary: Sharing links behave differently, and links that already exist may stop working.
sharing-restriction.Users: Existing anonymous links may expire or begin demanding sign-in. The person who shared it hears about it; the person who received it usually just gives up.
sharing-restriction.Admins: Audit existing anonymous links before changing the default — the change applies to new links, but link expiry and authentication requirements can reach existing ones depending on the setting.
sharing-restriction.Watchouts: Links embedded in published documents, email signatures, or a customer-facing portal are the ones that hurt. Search for them before enforcing.
sharing-restriction.Reversible: Yes for the setting; no for links already expired, which must be reissued.

device-gate.Summary: Access is refused from devices that do not meet the bar. Enrollment has to come first or people are locked out of their own work.
device-gate.Users: Personal and unenrolled devices lose access to corporate data. Users who work from a home machine will feel this immediately and strongly.
device-gate.Admins: Enroll and confirm compliance across the fleet before enforcing, then use report-only mode to find what is left. Report-only exists precisely so this change does not have to be a leap.
device-gate.Watchouts: Contractors, seasonal staff and anyone on a device the organization does not own are the population this locks out. Decide their path — enrollment, app protection policies, or a documented exception — before the policy goes to enforce.

device-config-change.Summary: Endpoint configuration changes. Most devices absorb it; a minority surface an application compatibility problem.
device-config-change.Users: Usually nothing. Where an application depends on the behavior being restricted, it stops working.
device-config-change.Admins: Pilot on a representative ring — including whatever the finance and clinical or line-of-business applications run on — before broad deployment. Devices apply it at their next check-in, so completion is measured in days, not minutes.
device-config-change.Watchouts: Older line-of-business software is the usual casualty. The failure is often a silent malfunction rather than an error message, so a pilot needs someone actually using the application, not just booting it.
device-config-change.Reversible: Yes, though devices need a check-in to pick up the reversal, and an offline device stays in the old state until it returns.

device-encryption.Summary: Drives are encrypted. The operation is transparent but the recovery key management is not optional.
device-encryption.Users: An initial encryption pass that slows the machine for a while. After that, nothing — unless a recovery prompt appears, which is alarming to anyone who has not been told it can happen.
device-encryption.Admins: Confirm recovery keys are escrowing to Entra ID before deploying broadly. An encrypted disk with no escrowed key is a data-loss event waiting for a firmware update.
device-encryption.Watchouts: Devices without a usable TPM will prompt for a startup PIN or fail the policy. Inventory hardware first; the answer for old hardware is replacement, not an exception.
device-encryption.Reversible: Decryption is possible but slow, and the reason to reverse is almost never good.

admin-elevation-friction.Summary: Privileged work needs an activation step first. Anything relying on standing admin rights stops working.
admin-elevation-friction.Admins: Activation, and where configured a justification or an approver, before privileged work. Real cost in an emergency at 2am, which is why break-glass accounts stay outside the policy.
admin-elevation-friction.Watchouts: Automation and scripts running under a standing-privilege account fail the moment the assignment becomes eligible rather than active. Move them to a service principal with scoped permissions before the change, not after the outage.

app-consent-friction.Summary: Users can no longer authorize applications against tenant data themselves; requests come to an administrator instead.
app-consent-friction.Users: A 'needs admin approval' message where an application used to just connect.
app-consent-friction.Admins: A request queue to work, with a response time people can live with. Without one, users route around it — and the route around it is shadow IT on a personal account, which is worse than what you restricted.
app-consent-friction.Watchouts: Existing consented applications keep working; this affects new grants. Review what is already consented separately, because that is where the risk already sits.

storage-retention.Summary: Data is kept longer or in more places. Costs money and creates discovery obligations.
storage-retention.Users: Content may become undeletable for the retention period — deleting appears to work but the item is preserved.
storage-retention.Admins: Storage consumption and, above certain tiers, license cost. Retained data is discoverable in litigation, which is a legal decision as much as a security one — retention longer than the organization's stated policy is its own liability.
storage-retention.Watchouts: Retention and deletion policies that overlap can conflict, and the more restrictive wins in ways that surprise people. Map them before adding another.
storage-retention.Reversible: The policy is reversible; data already preserved usually is not immediately releasable.

meeting-friction.Summary: Meetings behave differently for external and anonymous participants.
meeting-friction.Users: External attendees may wait in a lobby, be unable to join before an organizer, lose presentation rights, or be unable to join anonymously at all.
meeting-friction.Admins: Tell the people who run client-facing meetings before it changes, not after. Per-organizer meeting policies let sales and support keep a looser configuration where the business needs it.
meeting-friction.Watchouts: Webinars, client onboarding calls and public-facing sessions are where a lobby requirement becomes a business problem. Scope the policy rather than applying one setting tenant-wide.
meeting-friction.Reversible: Yes, immediately, and meetings already scheduled pick up the change.

data-classification-rollout.Summary: Users see labels, tips and blocks on their own content. Needs communication and a tuning period or it gets worked around.
data-classification-rollout.Users: Labels appear in Office applications; some actions produce a policy tip or a block with a justification prompt.
data-classification-rollout.Admins: Start in simulation or notify-only mode, read what it would have blocked, tune, then enforce. Skipping the simulation is how a DLP rollout blocks the payroll run on day one.
data-classification-rollout.Watchouts: Over-broad sensitive information types generate a flood of false positives, and the first hundred false blocks destroy the credibility of the whole program. Match on real document samples first.
data-classification-rollout.Reversible: Yes for the policy. Labels already applied to content persist and travel with the file.

dns-publication.Summary: A public DNS record changes. Fast to make, fast to reverse, and capable of breaking mail for the entire domain if it is wrong.
dns-publication.Admins: One record at the DNS host. Verify with an external lookup rather than trusting the registrar's interface, and check every service that sends on the domain's behalf is accounted for.
dns-publication.Watchouts: SPF has a hard limit of ten DNS lookups and exceeding it silently fails the whole record — including the parts that were working. Count the lookups, do not assume.

dns-certificate.Summary: Constrains which authorities may issue certificates for the domain. Wrong entries block future issuance, including renewals.
dns-certificate.Admins: Enumerate every certificate authority currently in use — including the ones inside a CDN, a load balancer or a hosting platform that renews automatically — before publishing.
dns-certificate.Watchouts: The failure appears at renewal, months later, as a certificate that cannot be issued and an outage on a service nobody associated with the DNS change.

power-platform-restriction.Summary: Existing flows and apps that cross the new boundary stop running, usually without telling their owner.
power-platform-restriction.Users: Makers lose self-service creation. Flows that combine a business connector with a personal or social one fail on their next run.
power-platform-restriction.Admins: Inventory existing flows and apps against the intended policy before applying it. The Power Platform admin center will show which would be affected — read it first.
power-platform-restriction.Watchouts: A broken flow fails quietly and its owner may have left the organization. Business processes silently stop; the discovery is a missing approval three weeks later.
power-platform-restriction.Reversible: Yes, and flows resume, but any run that was skipped is not replayed.

copilot-restriction.Summary: Copilot's behavior or availability changes for some users.
copilot-restriction.Users: Either lose access, or find Copilot declines to surface content it previously would have. Both read as 'Copilot is broken' unless explained.
copilot-restriction.Admins: Set expectations first. Copilot honors the permissions and labels that already exist, so restricting it usually exposes over-permissioned content rather than creating a new problem.
copilot-restriction.Watchouts: Over-shared SharePoint content is what Copilot makes visible. The right fix is the permissions, not the Copilot setting — restricting Copilot hides the symptom and leaves the exposure.

account-hygiene.Summary: Accounts get disabled, removed or unlicensed. Cheap to do, expensive to do to the wrong account.
account-hygiene.Users: The affected account loses access. If it was in use, that is an outage for the person holding it.
account-hygiene.Admins: Verify each account individually against sign-in activity and an owner before acting. Disable and wait before deleting — a fortnight of a disabled account costs nothing and catches the mistakes.
account-hygiene.Watchouts: Shared, service and break-glass accounts look dormant precisely because they are used rarely and deliberately. Those are the ones that must never be swept up in a bulk cleanup.
account-hygiene.Reversible: Disabling is reversible. Deletion is reversible for a limited window and then is not.

inventory-only.Summary: The finding is a list, not a change. Producing it affects nothing; acting on it is the change.
inventory-only.Admins: A worklist. Each entry needs an owner, a decision and a record of that decision — an entry left undecided reappears at every assessment and eventually stops being read.
inventory-only.Watchouts: Treating the list as the remediation. The list is evidence that work exists.

license-dependent.Summary: Primarily a license decision — the capability does not exist in the tenant until it is bought.
license-dependent.Users: Nothing until the feature is licensed and configured.
license-dependent.Admins: A purchase, then a configuration project. Do not scope the configuration effort as if the license were the whole cost; the license is the entry fee.
license-dependent.Watchouts: Buying the license and never configuring the feature is a common and expensive outcome that also produces a false sense of coverage.
license-dependent.Reversible: Configuration yes; the license commitment usually runs to term.

monitoring-integration.Summary: Log data flows to another system. No tenant behavior changes; cost and integration work do.
monitoring-integration.Admins: Connector configuration, credentials to rotate, and ingestion cost that scales with tenant size. Verify data is actually landing rather than that the connector reports healthy.
monitoring-integration.Watchouts: A silently stopped feed is worse than no feed, because it looks like coverage. Alert on the absence of data, not just on the data.

AAD-7.2.Summary: Creates two accounts that are deliberately outside every policy you just built. Getting this wrong either locks you out of the tenant or hands an attacker an unmonitored way in.
AAD-7.2.Watchouts: A break-glass account excluded from Conditional Access and never monitored is a permanent unguarded door. The exclusion is the point; the monitoring is what makes it safe. Do not create one without the other.
AAD-7.2.Reversible: Yes, but never remove the last usable path into the tenant.

AAD-3.1.Summary: Reduces the number of standing Global Administrators and moves them to cloud-only accounts.
AAD-3.1.Watchouts: Removing a Global Administrator that an integration authenticates as breaks that integration without warning. Check sign-in logs per account before removing the role, not after.
AAD-3.1.Reversible: Yes — the role can be reassigned — but a deleted account is a different matter.

EXO-2.6.Summary: Shared mailboxes stop being able to sign in directly, which is what they were never supposed to do.
EXO-2.6.Users: Anyone who has been signing into a shared mailbox with a shared password loses that route and must use delegated access from their own mailbox instead.
EXO-2.6.Watchouts: Shared passwords for shared mailboxes are common and undocumented. Find who is using them before blocking sign-in, or the first symptom is a department unable to work.

DEF-2.1.Summary: Applies Microsoft's Standard or Strict preset, which overrides most individually tuned anti-spam and anti-phishing settings.
DEF-2.1.Watchouts: Presets take precedence over custom policies. Any tuning done to solve a specific delivery problem is superseded silently, and the problem it solved comes back. Record what the custom policies were doing before switching.

PVW-1.1.Summary: Enables the tenant's audit log. No user-visible change, and it is not retroactive.
PVW-1.1.Watchouts: The reason this matters is an incident six months from now. Enabling it during an investigation does not produce the history the investigation needs — that history simply does not exist.

AAD-1.2.Watchouts: Enforce with a Conditional Access policy in report-only mode first and read the impact report. Service accounts, shared devices and anyone mid-travel are what report-only exists to surface. Break-glass accounts must be excluded before enforcement, and the exclusion must be monitored.

DNS-1.3.Summary: Tells the world's mail servers to quarantine or reject mail that fails authentication for your domain. It is the control that stops your domain being spoofed and the control most capable of stopping your own mail.
DNS-1.3.Watchouts: Publish p=none first and read aggregate reports until every legitimate sender passes SPF or DKIM — marketing platform, accounting package, e-signature service, the alerting system on the firewall. Only then move to quarantine, and to reject after that. Going straight to reject is the classic way to break a client's mail on a Friday.

EXO-8.2.Summary: Removing a transport rule that redirects mail externally stops an exfiltration path — and stops whatever legitimate process was relying on it.
EXO-8.2.Admins: Identify what consumes the redirected mail before deleting the rule. Archiving, e-discovery, a compliance mailbox and a ticketing intake all legitimately use CopyTo, and they break silently.
EXO-8.2.Watchouts: A rule that copies to an external address is sometimes a genuine, approved arrangement with an accountant or a managed service. Confirm ownership before removing; the finding is that it exists undocumented, not that it is automatically malicious.

EXO-8.1.Summary: Tightening or removing a mail connector changes how mail is routed. Get it wrong and mail stops flowing entirely.
EXO-8.1.Watchouts: Never delete a connector during business hours without knowing what routes through it. A hybrid Exchange server, a third-party filtering gateway and a scan-to-email appliance all depend on connectors, and removing one takes mail down for everybody it serves.

AAD-14.1.Summary: Rotating or removing an application credential breaks the integration using it the moment the old value stops working.
AAD-14.1.Users: Nothing directly — until an integration they depend on stops, which looks to them like the application being broken.
AAD-14.1.Watchouts: Add the new credential BEFORE removing the old one; Entra allows both to exist. Removing first guarantees an outage. Anything using the credential in a place you have forgotten (a scheduled task, a CI pipeline, a vendor system) surfaces only when it fails.

DEF-5.1.Summary: Expiring an allow entry means the sender, URL or file it covered goes back through normal filtering — which may block it again.
DEF-5.1.Watchouts: The entry existed for a reason, even if the reason is undocumented. Contact the owner before expiring it, or you re-create the original incident. Fix the underlying authentication problem (usually SPF/DKIM on the sender side) rather than re-adding the allow.

EXO-9.1.Summary: Putting every mailbox under retention or hold makes deleted mail undeletable for the retention period — which is the point, and also a discovery obligation.
EXO-9.1.Users: Nothing visible. Deleting mail appears to work; the copy is preserved where users cannot see it.
EXO-9.1.Watchouts: Retained mail is discoverable in litigation. Retaining longer than the organization own stated retention policy creates its own liability, so agree the period with whoever owns that policy before applying it. Litigation hold also needs Exchange Online Plan 2 — check licensing before promising it.

SPO-4.1.Summary: Extending departed-user OneDrive retention keeps leavers files longer. Costs storage and keeps their data in scope.
SPO-4.1.Watchouts: A retained OneDrive still counts toward tenant storage and still contains whatever the leaver had. Pair the change with an offboarding step that reassigns ownership, so retention is a safety net rather than an archive nobody reviews.
